summary: Reports on an IETF workshop held at MIT on 28 May 2008, organized by the area directors for real-time applications and infrastructure. It discussed delay and congestion problems caused by growing peer-to-peer traffic. It is an informational workshop report, not a protocol specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of experts met in a room to talk about how file-sharing programs crowd the internet. This is the written summary of what they said.

questions: how to reduce p2p network congestion
subtitle: Analysis of P2P congestion issues and proposed standardization paths from an IETF workshop.

tldr.problem: Large peer-to-peer file-sharing traffic volumes are causing network congestion and delay, particularly affecting real-time applications like VoIP and gaming on ISP networks with limited upstream capacity.
tldr.mechanism: A workshop convened by IETF area directors brought together ISPs, application providers, and researchers to discuss the technical problems and explore potential IETF standardization work. Discussions covered three main areas: improving peer selection through network information, new approaches to congestion control, and quality-of-service mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified several near-term standardization opportunities, including mechanisms for peers to learn network preferences and tools for congestion-aware application behavior. It established a foundation for ongoing IETF work on P2P and bandwidth-intensive applications.

today: RFC 5594 is an Informational workshop report. It has not been obsoleted. The work items identified have been pursued by the IETF community, with several RFCs resulting from the discussions, though the broader P2P congestion problem remains ongoing.

sections.title: The P2P Congestion Problem
sections.content:
Large ISPs increasingly experienced network congestion from peer-to-peer (P2P) file-sharing traffic. When network capacity approaches its limit, real-time applications such as Voice over IP (VoIP) and gaming suffer significant delays. To understand the technical problems and explore standardization solutions, the Real-time Applications and Infrastructure Area Directors organized the P2P Infrastructure workshop on May 28, 2008, at MIT.

The workshop brought together ISPs, P2P application providers, and network researchers. Its twofold goal was to understand what ISPs and end users experienced due to high P2P traffic volumes, and to identify where IETF standards work could help. Focus was on engineering solutions with near-term promise rather than research projects or proprietary approaches.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies that run the internet noticed that file-sharing programs were making everything slow. Experts gathered to figure out why and what the internet community could do about it.

sections.title: Why P2P Congests Cable Networks
sections.content:
Cable systems use the DOCSIS architecture, where a Cable Modem Termination System (CMTS) serves hundreds or thousands of customers over a hybrid fiber-coaxial network. Each CMTS has multiple domains with one downstream link and several upstream links. Bandwidth is the limiting resource.

A critical bottleneck occurs in the upstream direction. When many cable modems request transmission simultaneously, requests may collide, causing delays. Cable modem buffers can accumulate 1 to 4 seconds of delay. With P2P clients sending large volumes of upstream data continuously and piggybacking their next request on outgoing data, they dominate CMTS queues ahead of more interactive applications like VoIP, which transmit less frequently.

TCP flow fairness applies per flow rather than per modem, so a user running many P2P connections gets disproportionate bandwidth. ISPs attempted to manage this through traffic classification and dynamic service-level adjustment, but these approaches risk becoming a cat-and-mouse game as applications adapt to classification schemes.
sections.plainLanguage: Cable internet has limited space for data going back to the company. File-sharing programs monopolize this space with constant requests, while video calls and games only send small, occasional bursts.

sections.title: Improving Peer Selection Through Network Awareness
sections.content:
Peer selection is how a P2P application chooses which other peers to connect to. Today, peers largely ignore network topology and routing information, creating overlays that cross many ISP boundaries even when closer peers exist.

The workshop discussed several approaches to localization. Using Autonomous System (AS) numbers, peers could prefer to trade with others in the same AS, avoiding interdomain traffic costs. A case study of four popular BitTorrent swarms found 57% of peers were in ASes large enough that internal trading would avoid transit costs entirely, with potential 20% download-time improvements.

The P4P (Provider Portal for P2P Applications) framework proposes that ISPs expose link costs through a portal that applications query. Tests showed P4P reduced external traffic by 98% down to 50% while improving download times by 20%. Other proposals include multi-layer tracker architectures, ISP-hosted oracles to rank peer lists, and edge caches to localize content delivery. However, implementing these faces scaling challenges, legal liability concerns, and incentive alignment problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of connecting to random peers anywhere on the internet, programs could be smarter and prefer nearby peers. This would save ISP money and make downloads faster.

sections.title: New Congestion Control Approaches
sections.content:
Traditional TCP congestion control assumes cooperative endpoints but struggles under P2P traffic. The workshop identified two promising directions.

End-to-end scavenging involves P2P clients measuring their own delay (separating propagation from queuing) and adjusting transmission to keep queuing delay small, effectively yielding to competing traffic. BitTorrent implemented this, and the P4P framework supports marking traffic as bulk or time-sensitive, allowing applications to adjust behavior based on network feedback.

Longer-term, weighted congestion control could allow hosts to give interactive applications higher priority than bulk transfers, implemented through socket APIs without requiring network changes. Unlike Diffserv, this keeps control with users rather than ISPs and avoids proprietary classification. Both approaches require metrics (such as cost equal to unserved data) to prevent gaming the system.
sections.plainLanguage: File-sharing programs could be written to notice when the network is busy and slow down, letting important calls and games go through first.

sections.title: Quality of Service and Long-Term Solutions
sections.content:
Short-term ISP solutions like deep packet inspection to throttle P2P traffic risk becoming ineffective as applications evolve. QoS mechanisms may better address the problem structurally.

Differentiated Services Code Points (DSCP) [RFC2474] let edge devices mark packets with desired service levels. Devices inside the network honor these markings without remembering flow state. DSCP already has equipment support and wide enterprise deployment. It could facilitate usage-based charging where premium pricing for real-time traffic shapes user behavior.

However, DSCP faces deployment hurdles. The lack of uniform code points across networks complicates interoperability—for example, Windows Vista marks voice as CS7 (router priority), requiring network-wide re-marking. ISPs lack mechanisms to verify each others' markings and thus distrust them. Long-term solutions require either agreement on standardized code points or alternative mechanisms for expressing congestion across domain boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Rather than fighting about which data matters most, networks could label packets with their priority, and everyone could agree on what those labels mean.

sections.title: IETF Standardization Opportunities
sections.content:
The workshop identified several near-term standardization work items. For peer selection, the IETF could standardize mechanisms for clients to query their ISP's peering preferences and for discovering local trackers, caches, or oracles. Standardized peer ranking formats could reduce custom development.

For congestion control, investigating very deferential end-to-end congestion control for delay-tolerant applications merits protocol definition. An informational document on applications that open multiple TCP connections would help implementers understand flow fairness issues.

Longer-term, a design team could assess congestion in the broader context of massive bandwidth-use increases, not just P2P. Critical questions remain about swarm distributions, incentive alignment between ISPs and applications, and verification of shared information. Solutions must benefit all parties—applications, ISPs, and subscribers—or they will not gain traction.
sections.plainLanguage: The internet community could write standards for how networks and applications talk to each other about preferences and traffic limits, and how applications behave responsibly when the network is crowded.
